clue.text: Receiving repair damaged plant

indicators.note: something damaged is knocked out of shape, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A repair job on something that was received has made a plant worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' rearranges all fifteen letters of RECEIVING REPAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: A North American climber with leaves that turn red in autumn is a familiar garden plant.

clue.text: That may be seen as evil involving sister, say

indicators.note: to involve here is to wrap around, so the word for evil holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: something regarded as evil is vile, wicked
a sister is an example of a sib, a sibling

explanation.surface: Something is noticed as wicked because it drags in a nun or a sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sister, say' is an example signal: a sister is one kind of sibling, and SIB is the short form covering brother or sister.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perceptible to the eye, able to be noticed, is exactly what this adjective describes.

clue.text: Name of old boy, one in service

indicators.note: in puts the three single letters inside the abbreviation for the service

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy, one of the armed services
B is short for boy, as in births columns
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An old boy of the school is named as someone serving in the forces.
explanation.walkthrough: Not 'old boy' as one unit: O (old), B (boy) and I (one) sit inside RN, the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a common given name for a man, as with Robin Hood.

clue.text: Such expressions may be meaningless, academic admitted

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so the word for meaningless takes the degree inside it

parts.note: idiotic means senseless, meaningless
an MA, a Master of Arts, is an academic

explanation.surface: An academic concedes that some sayings may make no sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meaningless' looks like a comment on the expressions, but it is the word the academic goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Idioms are fixed phrases whose sense differs from their words, so expressions of that kind are described by this adjective.

clue.text: Learned head missing — say again

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, which here goes

parts.note: learned, well-read, means literate

explanation.surface: A scholar who has lost his head keeps repeating himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head missing' drops the first letter, L, from LITERATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To repeat or restate something is the plain synonym here, used often in mathematics and speech.

clue.text: Article collected by players ahead of a card game

indicators.note: ahead of puts the players-and-article piece before the final letter in the down entry
collected by means gathered inside, so the players take the article in

parts.note: the cast is the set of players in a show
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Players gather up an item before sitting down to a game of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'players' are actors in a show, the cast, not card players.
explanation.definitionFit: A rummy-style game played with two packs, popular in the mid-twentieth century, is the card game meant.

clue.text: Rest for artist after rest left

indicators.note: after says the letter for left comes behind the word for rest

parts.note: to rest is to ease off; ease is rest

explanation.surface: A painter needs a break after a rest has just finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' does two jobs in different senses: a support in the definition, relaxation in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist's stand holds the canvas, so it is a support or rest for the work.

clue.text: Father in French capital wants us raised together

indicators.note: in puts the word for father inside the city's name

parts.note: Paris is the capital of France
pa is a familiar word for father

indicators.note: in a down entry raised means read upwards, so the two letters run backwards

explanation.surface: A father in Paris wants the family to be brought up together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' suggests bringing up children, but in a down entry it turns the little word upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin phrase means side by side, at an equal rate, which is moving in step together.

clue.text: Managed to eat crackers before a period of fasting

indicators.note: to eat is to take inside, so the word for managed swallows the rest

parts.note: to run a business is to manage it, so managed is ran

indicators.note: before puts the word for crackers ahead of the article

parts.note: crackers, slang for crazy, means mad

explanation.surface: Someone got through eating crackers just before a fast began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crackers' looks like biscuits but is British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth month of the Islamic calendar is observed with fasting from dawn to dusk.

clue.text: Reserve team, lower

parts.note: a sub, a substitute, is a reserve player
a side is a team

explanation.surface: A reserve team is ranked lower than the first eleven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lower' reads as an adjective in the surface but is a verb, to sink or settle.
explanation.definitionFit: To sink down or settle, as water levels do, is to go lower, used as a verb.

clue.text: Boy returning with temperature given strange patent remedy

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the word for boy is read backwards

parts.note: a son is a boy
rum is old British slang for odd, strange

explanation.surface: A boy comes home with a fever and is given an odd quack medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: SON backwards gives NOS. RUM meaning strange is British; it has nothing to do with the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A quack cure or secret-formula medicine sold by its maker is the original sense of the word.

clue.text: Bars accepting foreign money? Certainly not

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the word for bars holds the other letters

parts.note: to bar is to ban, so bars are bans

indicators.note: foreign means strange or alien, so the letters of the word after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Do pubs take foreign currency? Absolutely not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' looks like pubs but is the verb sense, prohibitions.
explanation.definitionFit: An emphatic refusal or denial, an idiom meaning not in the least, matches the definition.

clue.text: Left work by editor, made strides

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: An editor has left a job and is making great progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made strides' looks like making progress but means running with long steps.
explanation.definitionFit: To run with long bounding steps is literally to make long strides.

clue.text: Section of government — it leaked name

indicators.note: Section of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Part of the government has leaked someone's name to the press.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is governm-ENT IT LE-aked.
explanation.definitionFit: To call something by a title, to give it a designation, is to name it, a verb sense.

clue.text: Musician in bad temper following tense game

indicators.note: following places the rearranged letters after the tense-and-game pieces

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
RU is rugby union, a game

indicators.note: bad means faulty, so the letters of the word after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A musician loses his temper after a nervy match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tense' looks like nervy but is the grammar term; the game is rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who plays a brass horn is one kind of musician, so this is an example of the definition.

clue.text: Skilled worker, one devoted to a cause, heading off

indicators.note: heading off means the head, the first letter, goes

parts.note: a partisan is a committed supporter of a cause

explanation.surface: A skilled worker who backs a cause is setting off somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' looks like leaving but removes P from PARTISAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A craftsman who works with the hands, such as a potter or carpenter, is a skilled worker.

clue.text: Examine striker, international

parts.note: to test is to examine
a match is struck to light it, so it is a striker

explanation.surface: Assess a forward who plays for the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'striker' wants to be a footballer; it is the thing struck on a matchbox. 'international' is a noun, a game between national teams.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket or rugby game between national sides is an international fixture.

clue.text: Club employee has energy bar, ultimately

parts.note: to have bounce is to be lively, full of energy

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter of the word for a counter is taken

explanation.surface: A nightclub worker is full of energy at the bar at the end of the night.
explanation.walkthrough: BOUNCE (liveliness) is followed by R, the last letter of 'bar'.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorman who keeps order at a nightclub is an employee of the club.

clue.text: Phone in bar over to rear

indicators.note: in puts the word for phone inside the reversed pub
over means turned over, so the word for a bar runs backwards

parts.note: a pub is a bar
to ring is to phone

explanation.surface: Call the pub and pass it over to the back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rear' is not the back but a verb, to raise children.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise children, to nurture and educate them, is the sense of the verb rear here.

clue.text: One taking stock of leader crossing street

indicators.note: crossing here means going across another, so the leader is spread around the street

parts.note: a ruler is a leader

explanation.surface: A leader crossing the road is checking inventory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking stock' suggests counting goods; here the stock is livestock, stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: A cattle thief makes off with livestock, so this person literally takes stock.

clue.text: View across centre of Hull, and river

indicators.note: across means lying around, so the word for view goes either side of the middle letters

parts.note: a vista is a view

indicators.note: the centre of a four-letter word is its two middle letters

explanation.surface: A view over the middle of Hull and its river.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is a city in northern England on the Humber; only its middle letters are used here.
explanation.definitionFit: The longest river in Poland, flowing through Warsaw to the Baltic, is this one.

clue.text: Brave, secure up in tank

indicators.note: in places the reversed word inside the tank

parts.note: a vat is a large tank

indicators.note: in a down entry up means read upwards, so the word for secure runs backwards

parts.note: to nail something is to secure it

explanation.surface: A brave soldier makes himself secure inside a tank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tank' suggests the army, but here it is a large container for liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: Courageous and bold, as a hero is, is the plain synonym here.

clue.text: Occasionally employed by New York newspaper?

definitions.meaning: occasionally means now and then, sometimes
working at the Times, as a staffer of that daily would be; the question mark flags the playful second reading

explanation.surface: Someone only sometimes works for a Manhattan paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase into two words: at the Times, the New York daily.
explanation.definitionFit: Now and then means sometimes; and working for the paper places a person at that office.

clue.text: Popular place makes contribution

parts.note: in means fashionable, popular
to place something is to put it

explanation.surface: A trendy venue earns its share of the takings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place' looks like a noun but is the verb, to put.
explanation.definitionFit: A share of effort, ideas or resources added to a project is someone's contribution.

clue.text: Tailor's initial trick, we hear, making trousers

indicators.note: initial means first, so only the opening letter of the word before it is used
we hear says the word for trick is to be heard, not read, and spelt by its sound

parts.note: a ruse is a trick

explanation.surface: A tailor's opening trick is said to produce a pair of trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: T, the first letter of 'Tailor's', is followed by REWS, which sounds like RUSE. Trews are close-fitting tartan trousers from Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartan trousers worn in Scotland, often by Highland regiments, are a kind of trousers.

clue.text: Book bargains here, and manuscript, item to be auctioned

parts.note: a sale is where bargains are found
a lot is an item put up at auction

explanation.surface: A book bought cheaply here, along with a handwritten copy and an auction piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb, to reserve; it is the definition, a Stephen King vampire novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen King's second novel, a 1975 vampire story about a small Maine town, is the book.

clue.text: Row over new type of cloth

indicators.note: in a down entry over means above, so the word for row sits on top of the letter for new

parts.note: a line is a row

explanation.surface: A dispute arises over a novel kind of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like a quarrel but means a line.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabric woven from flax is a common example of cloth.

clue.text: Turned on about revised rate? Don't be so naive

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the turned word goes around the rearranged letters
turned means turned round, so the word for on is read backwards

parts.note: in cricket the on side is also called the leg side, so on can mean leg

indicators.note: revised means altered, so the letters of the word after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone was excited by an altered rate, and is told to grow up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is the cricket term: the on side of the field is also called the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: A brusque idiom telling someone to face facts and stop being unrealistic fits the plea not to be naive.

clue.text: Not many bothered? It's just the opposite

indicators.note: bothered means flustered, mixed up, so the letters of the two words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Few people cared? Quite the reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: A word with the reverse meaning of another, as hot is to cold, is just the opposite.

clue.text: Savoury snack in packs, strong and rich when crunched

indicators.note: crunched means crushed and broken up, so the letters of the words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A savoury nibble sold in bags, strongly flavoured and rich to bite into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crunched' rearranges the letters of PACKS STRONG RICH. These are fried pieces of pork rind sold in British pubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Crisp deep-fried pieces of pig skin, a pub favourite in Britain, are a savoury snack.
